title: Kloster block
subtitle: The counted satin-stitch units that frame every hardanger cut area
excerpt: Kloster blocks are groups of five satin stitches worked over four fabric threads on evenweave linen. They form the structural border of hardanger embroidery, and threads may only be cut once every block is complete. Getting these units right is the foundation of the whole technique.
sourceNotes: Standard hardanger technique documented in Mary Gostelow's Embroidery (1977), Vine and Hardanger by Elsie Svennas, and widely in counted-thread needlework references. No single originator.

content.text: A kloster block is a group of five satin stitches worked side by side, each stitch spanning four threads of evenweave fabric. Blocks are placed in a counted grid, always at right angles to one another, so that pairs of blocks face each other across each square that will later be cut open. Nothing is cut until every block in the design is finished.

items.label: Thread
items.value: Perle cotton no 5 for kloster blocks; perle cotton no 8 for bars and fillings

items.label: Scissors
items.value: Small, sharp embroidery scissors with pointed tips for cutting threads later

items.label: Hoop or frame
items.value: Slate frame or 15-20 cm hoop to keep fabric taut

content.text: Secure the thread on the back of the fabric with two small stitches in an area that will be covered. Come up at the left edge of the block. Each stitch in the block covers exactly 4 fabric threads; the five stitches together cover 4 threads wide. Count carefully before placing the needle.

Work the five satin stitches from left to right, keeping them parallel and flat. Each stitch goes in at the top and comes up at the bottom of the same 4-thread span, one thread to the right of the last. The finished block is 5 stitches wide and 4 threads tall.

The next block that shares a corner with this one runs perpendicular. Turn the fabric 90 degrees in your mind: the new block's stitches will span 4 threads in the other direction, and the two blocks meet at a shared hole in the fabric. This shared corner point is where the right-angle relationship forms.

Continue placing all blocks in the design before doing anything else. Check that every area to be cut is fully enclosed by blocks on all four sides. Only when every block is complete may you cut the threads inside the enclosed squares. Cut parallel to the satin stitches, directly next to the edge of a block, never under it.
After cutting, withdraw the short thread ends carefully with the tip of the tapestry needle. The remaining threads form bars that are then worked with

items.symptom: Blocks are uneven or the stitches fan out
items.cause: The needle is going into a different number of threads on each stitch, or the fabric is not held taut
items.fix: Count each stitch before placing it. Use a frame to keep the linen under even tension. Each stitch must span the same 4 threads.

items.symptom: A cut thread slips under a block edge and frays
items.cause: Scissors were inserted at an angle or the cut was made before all bordering blocks were complete
items.fix: Always complete every block that encloses a square before cutting anything. Cut parallel to the satin stitches and as close to the block as possible without catching it.

items.symptom: Blocks do not meet at right angles at their corners
items.cause: Block placement was miscounted, so two adjacent blocks do not share the correct corner hole
items.fix: Mark the grid lightly with a water-soluble pen before starting. Check that the corner hole is shared by counting from a fixed reference point on each block.
